title: The Third Window
subtitle: The Legend of Lucien Vaire
teaser: For seven years, a gutter thief learned the sword through a window of the Academy of Saint-Ombre that never quite latched. He thought he was stealing the lessons.

sections.heading: I. The Ledge
paragraphs: The Academy of Saint-Ombre had twelve tall windows facing the harbour, and the third from the left never latched.

Lucien Vaire found it the summer he was nine, running from a sailor whose purse he had just lifted. He went up a drainpipe, along a ledge no wider than his hand, and lay flat under the sill. When he looked down through the glass, he forgot the sailor completely.
Below him, in a long hall of pale oak and brass lamps, two young lords were crossing blades faster than he could follow.
Saint-Ombre was a port city of fencers, and the Academy on the hill was where gentlemen were made. Nobody from the gutters ever went inside. Nobody had said anything about the ledge.

He came back every night for seven years. Through the open crack he learned the words first. Advance. Retreat. Lunge. Prise de fer, the taking of the blade. That one made sense to him straight away. He had been taking things since he could walk.
Afterwards, up on the rooftops, he practised with a broom handle stolen from a laundry, lunging at chimney pots.

The best fencer under that window was Thibault Morvane, a duke’s son two years older than Lucien. Before every lunge he gave a tiny bounce on his back foot, like a man about to hop a puddle. Lucien hated him in the plain, complete way you can only hate someone you are copying. He copied everything, down to the bounce.

At sixteen, he stole a sword from a carriage outside the Academy gates, where someone had left the door unlatched. Its hilt swept around the hand like a cage of silver vines. He took it the way he took everything, as if it were already his and he was only collecting it.
The next morning he walked into the fish market, where Thibault, now champion of the Academy, ate oysters every Sunday. He drew the sword and challenged him in front of half the city.

sections.heading: II. The Fish Market
paragraphs: Thibault looked at the skinny boy with yellow hair and a torn shirt, then at the sword, and smiled like someone hearing a good joke.
“Who taught you to hold that?”
“You did,” said Lucien. “You just didn’t know it.”
Thibault laughed and drew. “Then let me finish the lesson.”

He could have ended it in a second. He made it last a minute. He cut the buttons off Lucien’s shirt one by one and flicked them into the crowd. He disarmed him twice and kicked the sword back to him, hilt first. The fishwives laughed until they had to sit down.
The third time, he put Lucien on his back in the fish scales, laid the point under his chin, and said, loud enough for the whole market, “Go home, thief. Wherever that is.”
Then he turned to bow, and reached into his sleeve for his handkerchief to wipe the blade, and it wasn’t there.
Lucien, still lying in the fish scales, held up the handkerchief and waved it.
The market went silent. Then it roared.
The loudest laugh came from an old woman in black with a silver-headed cane. She walked over and looked down at him. “That,” she said, pointing the cane at the sword, “is mine.”
Everyone knew Master Ysolde. She had won the Queen’s Tournament twice before most of that market was born. Thibault went pale and bowed. She didn’t look at him.
“Do you know what that sword cost?” she asked Lucien.
“No.”
“Three hundred crowns. A servant at my academy earns four a year. Work it out.”
He couldn’t. He had never needed to count higher than a purse.
“Seventy-five years,” said Ysolde. “Get up. Find a broom.”
By evening every noble family at the Academy had written to complain. “He’s a servant,” Ysolde told them, while Lucien swept around their boots. “Servants sweep. Would you like him to stop?”

sections.heading: III. The Servant’s Green
paragraphs: The Academy’s servants wore green livery and a long green cloak. Lucien’s had belonged to a footman a head taller, and it dragged along the floor behind him.
“You’ll grow,” said Ysolde.

By day he swept. The hall was floored in diamond-shaped boards, and Ysolde sat by the windows calling out how she wanted it done. Two diamonds forward. One back. Cross. Turn. It was three months before he noticed she was teaching him footwork.
By night, when the lords had gone home, she lit two lamps and took down the practice blades. She raised her blade, tilted her head like a lady at a ball, and said, “Shall we dance?”
“It isn’t dancing,” he said, the first night. “It’s fighting.”
“That’s why you lose,” said Ysolde, and rapped him on the ear.

She was seventy-one, with a bad hip, and she hardly moved. Everything else was theatre: a flick of the cuff, a turn of the head, a bored sigh. While he watched the theatre, the point came in straight.
“Everything the left hand does is a lie,” she told him. “The cloak, the cuff, the face. Good. You’re a thief. Lie beautifully. Then go straight.”

So she taught him the cloak, an old street style the Academy had thrown out as vulgar. He learned to swirl the green hem across a man’s eyes the way he used to bump a shoulder in a crowd, and to send the point home while the man watched the cloth.

“Prise de fer,” she said one night, binding his blade and lifting it out of his hand like a cup off a table. “Take the blade. Then coup droit, the straight blow. Take, then go straight. That’s all fencing is. The rest is dancing.”

She called her pupils her heirs, and said most of them were a disappointment. By lamplight, one by one, Lucien outfenced them all. Only Thibault refused to cross blades with him. “I don’t fence the staff,” he said, and walked past Lucien every morning as if he were a coat stand. But he started checking his sleeve.

Every midsummer, the champion of the Queen’s Tournament won the right to open the Queen’s ball with any partner in the room. Thibault had won it every year since he was old enough. He always chose a duchess.
“I opened that ball twice,” Ysolde said one night. “I’d like to dance it once more before they bury me. Nobody asks old women.”
“Then I’ll win it,” said Lucien, “and I’ll ask you.”
“It’s open to sworn members of a fencing house. They mean noblemen.”
“Does it say noblemen?”
“No,” Ysolde said slowly. “It says sworn members. And a servant in livery is sworn to his house.” She tapped the green cloth at his collar with her cane. “Don’t you ever take that off.”

sections.heading: IV. The Queen’s Ball
paragraphs: At twenty-two, Lucien became the first servant ever named in the Queen’s Tournament. Half the nobility walked out. The other half stayed to watch him lose.

He didn’t. On the last night of midsummer he stood under the palace chandeliers, in green, across from Thibault Morvane. Ysolde watched from the gallery. She was seventy-seven and had not left her chair in a month, except to come here.
Thibault had done his homework. He ignored the cloak, the cuff, the face. He watched only the point, and every time it came in straight, his blade was waiting. Four touches to two, in a bout to five.
“You still fence like a thief,” Thibault said.
“I am a thief.”
“I know. I’ve been watching my sleeve.”

Lucien took the next touch, and the one after. Four all. Thibault set his feet for the lunge that had won him every final he had ever fenced: the one Lucien had watched through a window at nine and copied for seven years, down to the last detail.
Down to the bounce.
Lucien saw it. He took Thibault’s blade the way he had taken the handkerchief, as if it were already his. Then he went straight.
His point touched Thibault an inch below the collar, and the champion’s top button sprang off and went skittering across the marble to the Queen’s feet. She picked it up and laughed.
Thibault stared at it for a long moment. Then he gave Lucien the full salute, blade to brow, that a gentleman gives only to an equal.
The musicians lifted their bows. Lucien crossed the floor in his servant’s green, past the duchesses, past the Queen herself, up the gallery steps to an old woman with a cane, and bowed.
“Shall we dance?”
For six years she had asked him that every night. He had never once asked her.

Ysolde handed her cane to the nearest person, who happened to be Thibault, and took Lucien’s arm. They danced the slow pavane while she counted the steps under her breath, the way she used to call them out over his broom. She weighed almost nothing.
“The third window,” she said, halfway through. “On the harbour side.”
He missed a step.
“You thought the latch was broken. It wasn’t. I left it open and oiled the hinges, for forty years, for any child who climbed up there. You were the only one who kept coming back.”
“And the carriage?” he said, when he could. “The door left unlatched?”
“I’m old,” said Ysolde. “I forget things.”

She died that winter in her chair by the third window, with the shutters open. She left the Academy to her heirs, who were outraged to find it came with a servant they could not dismiss. She left Lucien the sword, with a card tied to the hilt in her spiky hand: “Paid in full. Keep dancing.”

sections.heading: V. The Green Flourish
paragraphs: He won the Queen’s Tournament three times, the first commoner ever to win it. Thibault was across the strip in every final. They have supper together after each one. Thibault pays, and keeps a hand on his sleeve all evening.
After the third, the Queen offered him a knighthood, and an end to the servant’s green forever. He bowed very low.
“Thank you, Majesty. But a title would only ruin the cape.”
So by law he is still a servant of the Academy, and when he is home he still sweeps the hall, in a green cloak that no longer drags.

In the rings they call him the Green Flourish: the swirl of green across your eyes, the flick of the cuff, all that bright, ridiculous theatre, and inside it the one straight line you never saw. When he parries, he takes your blade and comes straight down it, and there is no parry for that. Ysolde called it “that cheap business with the curtains,” and was enormously proud of it.
He came to the duelling rings because nobody at home would dance with him any more, and because in the rings nobody reads your livery.

And in every town there are children who can’t pay to get in, pressing their faces to the gaps in the fence, holding sticks. Before every bout Lucien walks the fence until he finds a loose board. If there isn’t one, he loosens one. During the fight he drifts to that side and slows down a little, so they can see his feet.
Then he turns to whoever is waiting across the ring, raises the sword an old woman once forgot on the seat of a carriage, and tilts his head like a man at a ball.
“Shall we dance?”
